title: Idioms, proverbs and spoken Ukrainian
objectives: I can say what the words of a Ukrainian idiom literally say, what the idiom means and when to use it, for six common idioms.
I can recognize the patterns of Ukrainian proverbs, such as 'що..., те...', 'хто..., той...' and an imperative with 'по́ки' or 'по́ки не', and use three proverbs at the right moment.
I can add emphasis, surprise, doubt and insistence with the particles 'ж', 'же', 'хіба́', 'невже́', 'адже́', 'таки́', 'ну' and 'от'.
I can recognize the features of everyday speech, such as dropped verbs, emphatic word order and the interjections 'ой' and 'ого́', and choose between conversational and formal style.
I can explain why the particle is written 'ж' after a vowel and 'же' after a consonant, and how 'ого́', 'невже́' and 'адже́' are pronounced.

vocabulary.note: 'Би́ти' is 'to beat' or 'to hit' ('б’ю', 'б’єш', 'вони́ б’ють'; imperative 'бий'). 'Байдики́' is a plural word that lives on only in this idiom and has no meaning of its own today, so the gloss keeps it as it is. The idiom is informal and a little disapproving: it is said of someone who should be working.

example.source: Stop lazing about and help me!

vocabulary.note: 'Ки́нути' is the perfective 'to throw' ('ки́ну', 'ки́неш'; imperative 'кинь'), and its imperfective partner is 'кида́ти'. 'О́ком' is the instrumental of 'о́ко', the means: one quick throw of the eye. What is looked at follows 'на' with the accusative. The idiom is neutral and fits both speech and writing.

example.target: Мо́жна ки́нути о́ком на ваш докуме́нт?
example.source: May I take a look at your document?
example.source_literal: Possible to-throw by-eye on your document?

vocabulary.note: 'Розли́ти' is a perfective verb, 'to pour out' or 'to spill', built from 'ли́ти', to pour, and the prefix 'роз-', apart. The picture is of friends so close that not even water poured between them would separate them. The idiom is the whole predicate of a sentence without a subject: the friends are its object, in the accusative, and nothing in the idiom changes. It is informal and affectionate.

example.target: Окса́ну й Оле́ну водо́ю не розли́ти.
example.source_literal: Oksana and Olena by-water not to-pour-apart.

vocabulary.note: Said of someone who is at ease and skilled in a place or an activity, often with 'почува́тися' or in a sentence without a verb: 'Він тут як ри́ба у воді́.' It is praise, and neutral in register. The 'у' stays before 'воді́' after any word, because 'у' is always written before 'в'.

example.target: На ку́хні Гали́на почува́ється як ри́ба у воді́.
example.source: Halyna is in her element in the kitchen.
example.source_literal: In kitchen Halyna feels like fish in water.

vocabulary.note: 'Ра́да' is an old word for counsel, and today it also means a council: the parliament of Ukraine is 'Верхо́вна Ра́да', the Supreme Council. The person who copes is the subject; what they cope with is in the dative, and 'собі́', to oneself, is added for coping on one's own. The perfective is 'да́ти ра́ду' ('дам', 'даси́'). After a negated verb the noun is in the genitive: 'не дава́ти ра́ди'. The idiom is neutral in register.

example.target: Ця робо́та важка́, але́ я дам собі́ ра́ду.
example.source: This job is hard, but I'll manage.
example.source_literal: This work difficult, but I will-give to-self counsel.

vocabulary.note: 'Трима́ти' is 'to hold' ('трима́ю', 'трима́єш'), and 'язи́к' is 'tongue'. In this idiom the tongue is in the accusative 'язика́', a form that looks like the genitive and that several idioms about the tongue keep. 'За зуба́ми' is 'за' with the instrumental plural of 'зуб', for position. The idiom is informal: it is friendly advice to a friend and rude to anyone else.

example.target: Ті́льки нікому́ не кажи́: трима́й язика́ за зуба́ми.
example.source: Just don't tell anyone; keep your mouth shut.
example.source_literal: Only to-nobody not say: hold tongue behind teeth.

vocabulary.note: 'Тихі́ше' is the comparative of 'ти́хо', quietly, here meaning 'more slowly', and 'да́лі' is the comparative of 'дале́ко', far. The 'ти' forms speak to anyone. It is said to someone who is rushing, and often only its first half is spoken.

example.target: Не тре́ба так шви́дко, Се́ме. Тихі́ше ї́деш, да́лі бу́деш.
example.source: There's no need to go so fast, Sam. More haste, less speed.
example.source_literal: Not necessary so quickly, Sam. Quieter you-go, further you-will-be.

vocabulary.target: Не кажи́ гоп, по́ки не переско́чиш.
vocabulary.source: don't count your chickens before they hatch
vocabulary.source_literal: not say hop, while not you-will-jump-over
vocabulary.note: 'Гоп' is an interjection shouted while jumping, and 'переско́чити' is the perfective 'to jump over', with 'пере-', across. 'По́ки не' with a perfective verb means 'until', and its 'не' negates nothing. It is said to someone who celebrates before the result is certain.

example.target: Ти ще не ви́грав, тому́ не кажи́ гоп, по́ки не переско́чиш.
example.source: You haven't won yet, so don't count your chickens before they hatch.
example.source_literal: You still not won, therefore not say hop, while not you-will-jump-over.

vocabulary.note: 'Посі́яти' is 'to sow' ('посі́ю', 'посі́єш') and 'пожа́ти' is 'to reap' ('пожну́', 'пожне́ш'), both perfective. 'Що' opens the first half and 'те' picks it up in the second; 'й' is the particle 'also', underlining 'те'. The proverb warns about the results of bad work, or praises good work that has paid off.

example.target: Ти бага́то працюва́ла, і от ти ма́єш нову́ робо́ту. Що посі́єш, те й пожне́ш.
example.source: You worked hard, and now you have a new job. You reap what you sow.
example.source_literal: You much worked, and there you have new work. What you-will-sow, that also you-will-reap.

vocabulary.note: It opens a question when the speaker doubts or is surprised, and expects the answer opposite to what the words say: 'Хіба́ ти не зна́єш?' expects that you do know.

example.target: Хіба́ він не прийде́ на вечі́рку?
example.source: Isn't he coming to the party?
example.source_literal: Surely he not will-come on party?

vocabulary.note: It opens a question, or stands alone, and shows surprise or disbelief at something that seems to be true: 'Невже́?' (Really?).

example.source: Is it really Friday tomorrow already?

vocabulary.note: It opens a clause and gives a reason that the listener already knows. It is as common in writing as in speech.

example.target: Ході́мо додо́му, адже́ за́втра на робо́ту.
example.source: Let's go home; we have work tomorrow, after all.
example.source_literal: Let's-go to-home, after-all tomorrow to work.

vocabulary.note: It stands before the word it stresses, usually the verb, and says that something happened despite doubts or obstacles. It never changes, and it is a different word from the pronoun 'таки́й', such.

example.source: You bought that jacket after all!

vocabulary.note: It stands right after the word it stresses and is said together with it, without stress. It is written 'ж' after a vowel and 'же' after a consonant. In a statement it means 'after all, you know'; in a question it insists; with an imperative it urges.

example.target: Ти ж зна́єш, що я люблю́ чай.
example.source_literal: You indeed know, that I love tea.

vocabulary.note: It opens a reply while the speaker thinks, urges someone on, or, with 'й', opens an exclamation: 'Ну й пого́да!' (What weather!).

example.target: Ну, я не зна́ю, що сказа́ти.
example.source: Well, I don't know what to say.

vocabulary.note: It points at something in speech, as 'ось' does, or sums up: 'От і все.' (That's all.). It is more conversational than 'ось'.

example.source: There, you see, I told you!

vocabulary.note: It shows admiring surprise at something big, numerous or impressive. Both vowels keep their full 'о' sound, and the 'г' is the voiced [ɦ].

example.source: Wow, there are so many people here!

vocabulary.note: It shows sudden surprise, fright, pain or dismay. It is one syllable, said [ɔj].

example.source: Oh, I left my keys at home!

dialogues.title: Sam's new idioms
dialogues.context: Taras, who now works in Lviv, is back in Kyiv for a few days. At Andrii's café Sam tries out on him the idioms he learned at the weekend. Sam and Taras say 'ти' to each other, and Andrii says 'ви' to his customers.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Приві́т, Се́ме! Що ти роби́в на вихідни́х?
lines.source: Hi, Sam! What did you do at the weekend?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Sam! What you did on weekend?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ну, я ці́лі вихідні́ бив байдики́. Ви́вчив два́дцять ідіо́м!
lines.source: Well, I lazed about the whole weekend. I learned twenty idioms!
lines.source_literal: Well, I whole weekend beat baidyky. Learned twenty of-idioms!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Як це? Би́ти байдики́ означа́є нічо́го не роби́ти.
lines.source: How's that? Lazing about means doing nothing.
lines.source_literal: How this? To-beat baidyky means nothing not to-do.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ой! Я хоті́в сказа́ти, що бага́то працюва́в.
lines.source: Oh! I meant to say that I worked a lot.
lines.source_literal: Oh! I wanted to-say, that much worked.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я так і ду́мав. Ти ж ніко́ли не б’єш байдики́.
lines.source: I thought so. You never laze about, after all.
lines.source_literal: I so also thought. You indeed never not beat baidyky.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: До́брий день, хло́пці! Що вам принести́?
lines.source: Hello, guys! What can I bring you?
lines.source_literal: Good day, guys! What to-you to-bring?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ ка́ву, будь ла́ска. І мо́жна ки́нути о́ком на меню́?
lines.source: A coffee for me, please. And may I glance at the menu?
lines.source_literal: To-me coffee, be kindness. And possible to-throw by-eye on menu?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Звича́йно, ось воно́.
lines.source: Of course, here it is.
lines.source_literal: Of course, here it.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Се́ме, ти вже де́сять хвили́н чита́єш меню́! Хіба́ це «ки́нути о́ком»?
lines.source: Sam, you've been reading the menu for ten minutes! Is that a glance?
lines.source_literal: Sam, you already ten of-minutes read menu! Surely this «to-throw by-eye»?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ой, я не те сказа́в?
lines.source: Oh, did I say the wrong thing?
lines.source_literal: Oh, I not that said?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Нічо́го, Се́ме. Ви тут як ри́ба у воді́, а ідіо́ми ще ви́вчите.
lines.source: Never mind, Sam. You're in your element here, and you'll learn the idioms yet.
lines.source_literal: Nothing, Sam. You here like fish in water, and idioms still will-learn.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! За мі́сяць я ви́вчу всі ідіо́ми.
lines.source: Thank you! I'll learn all the idioms in a month.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! Within month I will-learn all idioms.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Не кажи́ гоп, по́ки не переско́чиш.
lines.source: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
lines.source_literal: Not say hop, while not you-will-jump-over.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тара́се, ти ж зна́єш, що це прислі́в’я я вже ви́вчив!
lines.source: Taras, you know I've already learned that proverb!
lines.source_literal: Taras, you indeed know, that this proverb I already learned!

dialogues.title: News about Sofiia
dialogues.context: Oksana and Olena, friends who say 'ти' to each other, meet in the park. Olena has news about Sofiia, who was Taras's manager when he worked in Kyiv.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Окса́но, ти вже чу́ла нови́ну про Со́фію?
lines.source: Oksana, have you heard the news about Sofiia?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, you already heard news about Sofiia?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ні. Яку́ нови́ну?
lines.source: No. What news?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Вона́ таки́ звільни́лася!
lines.source: She did quit after all!
lines.source_literal: She still quit!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Невже́? Вона́ ж так люби́ла свою́ робо́ту.
lines.source: Really? But she loved her job so much.
lines.source_literal: Really? She indeed so loved her-own work.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Люби́ла, але́ вона́ до́вго мрі́яла працюва́ти в ба́нку.
lines.source: She did, but she had dreamed of working in a bank for a long time.
lines.source_literal: Loved, but she long dreamed to-work in bank.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: І де вона́ за́раз?
lines.source: And where is she now?
lines.source_literal: And where she now?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: У вели́кому ба́нку в це́нтрі, і в не́ї там два́дцять співробі́тників!
lines.source: At a big bank downtown, and she has twenty employees there!
lines.source_literal: In big bank in center, and at her there twenty of-employees!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ого́! А вона́ дасть собі́ ра́ду?
lines.source: Wow! But will she cope?
lines.source_literal: Wow! And she will-give to-self counsel?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Звича́йно. Вона́ там як ри́ба у воді́. Що посі́єш, те й пожне́ш: вона́ ж ду́же бага́то працюва́ла.
lines.source: Of course. She's in her element there. You reap what you sow: she worked very hard, after all.
lines.source_literal: Of course. She there like fish in water. What you-will-sow, that also you-will-reap: she indeed very much worked.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А Тара́с уже́ зна́є?
lines.source: And does Taras know yet?
lines.source_literal: And Taras already knows?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Звича́йно. Їх із Со́фією водо́ю не розли́ти, хоча́ він за́раз у Льво́ві.
lines.source: Of course. He and Sofiia are inseparable, even though he's in Lviv now.
lines.source_literal: Of course. Them with Sofiia by-water not to-pour-apart, although he now in Lviv.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А чому́ мені́ ніхто́ нічо́го не сказа́в?
lines.source: So why did nobody tell me anything?
lines.source_literal: And why to-me nobody nothing not said?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Бо Со́фія проси́ла, щоб ми трима́ли язика́ за зуба́ми.
lines.source: Because Sofiia asked us to keep our mouths shut.
lines.source_literal: Because Sofiia asked, so-that we held tongue behind teeth.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ой! А ти ж мені́ все розпові́ла!
lines.source: Oh! But you've just told me everything!
lines.source_literal: Oh! And you indeed to-me all told!

dialogues.title: Idioms in a letter?
dialogues.context: After class, Sam asks his teacher Iryna Petrivna whether he may use idioms in a letter to an employer; he says 'ви' to her. At the end Oksana joins them; she and Sam say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Іри́но Петрі́вно, мо́жна запита́ти? Чи мо́жна писа́ти ідіо́ми в листі́ до роботода́вця?
lines.source: Iryna Petrivna, may I ask something? Can I use idioms in a letter to an employer?
lines.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna, possible to-ask? Whether possible to-write idioms in letter to employer?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Мо́жна, Се́ме, але́ не всі. А які́ ідіо́ми?
lines.source: You can, Sam, but not all of them. Which idioms?
lines.source_literal: Possible, Sam, but not all. And which idioms?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Напри́клад: «Я на робо́ті як ри́ба у воді́ й ніко́ли не б’ю байдики́».
lines.source: For example: 'At work I'm in my element, and I never laze about.'
lines.source_literal: For example: «I on work like fish in water and never not beat baidyky».

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ой, Се́ме, у листі́ до роботода́вця так не пи́шуть.
lines.source: Oh, Sam, people don't write like that in a letter to an employer.
lines.source_literal: Oh, Sam, in letter to employer so not they-write.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Чому́? Хіба́ ці ідіо́ми пога́ні?
lines.source: Why? Are these idioms bad, then?
lines.source_literal: Why? Surely these idioms bad?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ні, вони́ га́рні, але́ розмо́вні. Їх ка́жуть дру́зям, а не роботода́вцеві.
lines.source: No, they're good, but they're conversational. You say them to friends, not to an employer.
lines.source_literal: No, they nice, but conversational. Them they-say to-friends, and not to-employer.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А що тоді́ писа́ти в листі́?
lines.source: Then what should I write in the letter?
lines.source_literal: And what then to-write in letter?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Пиші́ть про свій до́свід. А ідіо́ми кажі́ть дру́зям у кафе́.
lines.source: Write about your experience. Save the idioms for your friends at the café.
lines.source_literal: Write about your-own experience. And idioms say to-friends in café.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Зрозумі́в. До ре́чі, я хо́чу ви́вчити сто ідіо́м за ти́ждень!
lines.source: I see. By the way, I want to learn a hundred idioms in a week!
lines.source_literal: Understood. To thing, I want to-learn hundred of-idioms within week!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Тихі́ше ї́деш, да́лі бу́деш, Се́ме. Кра́ще вивча́йте п’ять ідіо́м на ти́ждень, але́ до́бре.
lines.source: More haste, less speed, Sam. Better to learn five idioms a week, but learn them well.
lines.source_literal: Quieter you-go, further you-will-be, Sam. Better learn five of-idioms per week, but well.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Се́ме, ти додо́му?
lines.source: Sam, are you off home?
lines.source_literal: Sam, you to-home?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, я в бібліоте́ку. А ти?
lines.source: No, I'm off to the library. And you?
lines.source_literal: No, I in library. And you?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я теж. Ну, ми пішли́! До поба́чення, Іри́но Петрі́вно!
lines.source: Me too. Right, we're off! Goodbye, Iryna Petrivna!
lines.source_literal: I too. Well, we went! Until seeing, Iryna Petrivna!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До поба́чення! І не би́йте байдики́!
lines.source: Goodbye! And don't laze about!
lines.source_literal: Until seeing! And not beat baidyky!

grammar.title: Idioms: what the words say, what they mean and how they are used
grammar.explanation:
An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning is not the sum of the meanings of its words. 'Би́ти байдики́' does not describe beating anything: it means 'to laze about'. Ukrainian grammar calls such a group 'фразеологі́зм', and in everyday speech people also say 'ідіо́ма'. This course gives every idiom in three separate ways:

- the literal rendering, which shows what the words say in the Ukrainian order: 'to-throw by-eye'
- the natural English equivalent: 'to glance'
- the use: who says it, to whom and in what situation

The literal rendering matters because the picture behind an idiom often explains it. In 'водо́ю не розли́ти' two friends are so close that water poured between them would not separate them. In 'ки́нути о́ком' the eye is thrown at something quickly and once, which is why the verb is perfective.

An idiom keeps its words and their order, but its grammar still works:

- The verb conjugates and agrees as usual: 'я б’ю байдики́', 'вона́ би́ла байдики́', 'Не бий байдики́!'.
- The verb has its aspect partner where the meaning allows it: 'дава́ти ра́ду' for coping in general or again and again, 'да́ти ра́ду' for one task managed: 'Я дам собі́ ра́ду.' (I'll manage.)
- The nouns keep the case they have in the idiom: 'о́ком' stays instrumental, and 'язика́ за зуба́ми' never changes.
- After a negated verb the noun of 'дава́ти ра́ду' goes into the genitive, as the object of a negated verb often does in Ukrainian: 'Він не дає́ ра́ди.' (He can't cope.)
- An idiom that is the whole predicate takes no subject: in 'Їх водо́ю не розли́ти.' the friends are the object 'їх', in the accusative.

A word of an idiom cannot be replaced by a word of similar meaning, because the idiom then stops being one. Nor can an English idiom be translated word for word and still be understood, so learn the Ukrainian picture instead.

Idioms are not all informal. 'Ки́нути о́ком', 'дава́ти ра́ду' and 'як ри́ба у воді́' are neutral and appear in newspapers. 'Би́ти байдики́' and 'трима́ти язика́ за зуба́ми' belong to conversation: said to a friend they are friendly, while said to a teacher or a stranger they sound rude.

The column in this unit's reading is about idioms with 'твари́ни', animals (singular 'твари́на'), and with 'части́ни ті́ла', parts of the body ('части́на', part, and 'ті́ло', body). The table also gives three idioms from it. In 'як кіт напла́кав' the perfective 'напла́кати' means 'to cry a quantity of tears'; in 'ру́ки не дохо́дять' the verb 'дохо́дити' is the imperfective of 'дійти́', to reach; in 'коли́ рак на горі́ сви́сне' the word 'рак' is a crayfish, 'гора́' a mountain and 'сви́снути' the perfective 'to whistle'.

grammar.title: Proverbs and their patterns
grammar.explanation:
A proverb, 'прислі́в’я', is a complete sentence that states a lesson about life: 'Що посі́єш, те й пожне́ш.' (You reap what you sow.) A saying, 'при́казка', is a shorter fixed phrase without a lesson of its own, such as the comparison 'як ри́ба у воді́'. Proverbs are old, so their grammar is compact, and a few patterns cover most of them.

The first pattern is two halves without a linking word. The first half states a condition or a cause, and the second the result, with no word for 'if': 'Тихі́ше ї́деш, да́лі бу́деш.' means 'if you go more quietly, you will get further'. Ukrainian punctuation usually separates such halves with a dash; this course writes a comma, because a speech engine reads every Ukrainian sentence in it aloud. The verbs are in the 'ти' form, which here means anyone, as English 'you' does in 'you never know'.

The second pattern is a pair of pointing words. The first half opens with a question word used as a relative word, and the second half picks it up with a form of 'той' or with 'так':

- 'що..., те...': 'Що посі́єш, те й пожне́ш.', literally 'what you-will-sow, that also you-will-reap'
- 'хто..., той...': 'Хто шука́є, той знахо́дить.' (Seek and you will find.) 'Шука́ти' is 'to look for', and 'знахо́дити' is the imperfective of 'знайти́'.
- 'як..., так...': 'Як дба́єш, так і ма́єш.' (You get what you put in.) 'Дба́ти' is 'to take care of things'.

The form of 'той' takes the case its own half needs. In 'Хто ра́но встає́, тому́ Бог дає́.' (The early bird catches the worm), where 'ра́но' is 'early' and 'Бог' is 'God', the word 'тому́' is the dative of 'той', 'to that one', and not the adverb 'тому́', therefore. The 'й' or 'і' after the pointing word is the particle 'і', 'also', which underlines it; it joins nothing.

The third pattern is an imperative followed by 'по́ки' and a time limit:

- Without 'не', 'по́ки' means 'while': 'Куй залі́зо, по́ки гаря́че.' (Strike while the iron is hot.) 'Куй' is the imperative of 'кува́ти', to forge, and 'гаря́че', hot, is the neuter of 'гаря́чий', agreeing with 'залі́зо', iron.
- With 'не' and a perfective verb in its future form, 'по́ки не' means 'until', and the 'не' negates nothing: 'Не кажи́ гоп, по́ки не переско́чиш.' (Don't say 'hop' until you have jumped over.)

The tenses follow aspect: the present for a truth that always holds ('шука́є', 'знахо́дить'), and the perfective future for one completed act ('посі́єш', 'пожне́ш', 'переско́чиш'). Other proverbs use the imperative with 'те, що' ('Не відклада́й на за́втра те, що мо́жна зроби́ти сього́дні.', where 'відклада́ти' is the imperfective of 'відкла́сти') or a plain statement ('Дру́зі пізнаю́ться в біді́.', where 'пізнава́тися' is 'to be recognized' and 'біда́' is 'trouble'). In conversation Ukrainians often say only the first half of a well-known proverb and let the listener complete it.

grammar.title: Particles of attitude: ж, же, хіба́, невже́, адже́, таки́, ну and от
grammar.explanation:
A particle is a small word that never changes its form and adds the speaker's attitude rather than new facts, as 'не' adds negation and 'чи' a question. Spoken Ukrainian is full of them. They do the work that English does with tone of voice, with tags such as 'don't you?' and with words such as 'really', 'after all' and 'still'. Without them the facts of a sentence stay the same, but its feeling is lost.

The particles of this unit, each with its place in the sentence:

- 'ж' or 'же' stands right after the word it emphasizes and is said together with it. In a statement it means 'after all, you know': 'Я ж каза́в!' (I told you!). In a question it insists: 'Де ж він?' (Where on earth is he?). With an imperative it urges: 'Ходи́ ж сюди́!' (Come over here, will you!).
- 'Хіба́' opens a question when the speaker doubts or is surprised, and expects the answer opposite to what the words say: 'Хіба́ ти не зна́єш?' (Don't you know? I thought you did.)
- 'Невже́' opens a question or stands alone, and shows surprise or disbelief at something that seems to be true: 'Невже́ це пра́вда?' (Is it really true?)
- 'Адже́' opens a clause and gives a reason the listener already knows: 'Візьми́ ку́ртку, адже́ хо́лодно.' (Take a jacket; it's cold, after all.) It is the one particle here that is just as common in writing.
- 'Таки́' stands before the word it stresses, usually the verb, and says that something happened despite doubts or obstacles: 'Вона́ таки́ прийшла́.' (She came after all.) It also appears in 'все-таки́', nevertheless, written with a hyphen and spelled 'усе́-таки́' after a consonant: 'Він усе́-таки́ прийшо́в.' (He came nevertheless.)
- 'Ну' opens a reply while the speaker thinks ('Ну, не зна́ю.'), urges ('Ну, ході́мо!'), or, followed by the particle 'й', opens an exclamation ('Ну й пого́да!', What weather!).
- 'От' points at something in speech, as 'ось' does ('От він!', There he is!), or sums up ('От і все.', That's all.).

'Хіба́' and 'невже́' are close, but they are not the same. 'Хіба́' questions what the words say: 'Хіба́ він ви́грав?' suggests that he did not win. 'Невже́' marvels at it: 'Невже́ він ви́грав?' suggests that he did, and that the speaker can hardly believe it.

The particle 'таки́' and the pronoun 'таки́й', such, are different words. 'Таки́й' agrees with a noun ('таки́й день', 'така́ ку́ртка'); 'таки́' has no 'й' and never changes.

The word-for-word glosses of this course render 'ж' and 'же' as 'indeed', 'хіба́' as 'surely', 'невже́' as 'really', 'адже́' as 'after-all', 'таки́' as 'still', 'ну' as 'well', 'от' as 'there' and the particle 'і' as 'also', except in 'Ну й...!', where it is 'and'.

grammar.title: Spoken Ukrainian: dropped verbs, emphatic word order and interjections
grammar.explanation:
Everyday speech leaves out what the situation makes clear, puts the most important word where it stands out, and colors the sentence with interjections. These features are normal in conversation and in informal messages, and formal writing avoids them.

A verb of motion is often left out when the direction is stated, because the direction already shows that someone is going somewhere:

- 'Ти куди́?' (Where are you off to?)
- 'Я додо́му.' (I'm off home.)
- 'Я до Оле́ни.' (I'm going to Olena's.)
- 'Ми в кіно́.' (We're off to the movies.)

'Додо́му' is an adverb meaning 'home' as a direction, written as one word from 'до' and 'до́му', the genitive of 'дім'. 'Вдо́ма' is home as a location.

A verb of speech is left out when a story quotes someone: 'А він мені́: «Ні!»' (And he says to me, 'No!'). The person spoken to is in the dative, and the words follow a colon inside «».

The perfective past of 'піти́' announces that you are leaving right now: 'Ну, я пішо́в!' or 'Ну, я пішла́!' (Right, I'm off!). The departure is presented as already done, because it will be done in a moment. It is often followed by 'до за́втра', see you tomorrow, literally 'until tomorrow'.

Word order is free in Ukrainian, and speech uses it for emphasis. The word that carries the feeling or the contrast comes first, and the new information comes last:

- 'Га́рна в тебе́ ку́ртка!' puts 'га́рна' first and means 'What a nice jacket you have!'
- 'Ка́ву я не п’ю, а чай п’ю.' puts the two drinks being contrasted first: 'I don't drink coffee, but I do drink tea.'

An interjection, 'ви́гук', expresses a feeling and is not part of the grammar of the sentence, so it stands alone or is set off by a comma:

- 'ой' for sudden surprise, fright, pain or dismay: 'Ой, я забу́в ключі́!' (Oh, I forgot my keys!)
- 'ого́' for admiring surprise at something big, numerous or impressive: 'Ого́, яка́ ри́ба!' (Wow, what a fish!)
- 'гоп' for a jump, as in the proverb 'Не кажи́ гоп...'

The right style depends on the listener. With friends and family, dropped verbs, particles and informal idioms make speech sound natural. With a teacher, an official or a stranger, whom you call 'ви', speak in full sentences and leave out informal idioms such as 'би́ти байдики́'. A formal letter uses none of these features except 'адже́'.

The story in this unit's reading is told in this spoken style. Its new words are:

- 'лови́ти ри́бу', to fish, literally 'to catch fish'
- 'спійма́ти', the perfective 'to catch' ('спійма́ю', 'спійма́єш')
- 'чек', a receipt

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ж and же, ого́, невже́, адже́ and the words of the idioms
grammar.explanation:
The particle 'же' has two spellings for the same reason as 'би' and 'б', and 'у' and 'в': Ukrainian prefers an even flow of vowels and consonants. After a word that ends in a vowel it is written 'ж', and after a word that ends in a consonant, 'же':

- 'я ж', 'ти ж', 'де ж', 'вона́ ж', 'Оле́на ж', 'ходи́ ж'
- 'він же', 'Тара́с же', 'їх же'

Either way it has no stress and is said together with the word before it, as if it were that word's last sound or syllable. The 'ж' at the end of 'ти ж' [tɪʒ] stays voiced, as a voiced consonant does at the end of a Ukrainian word ('хліб').

'Ого́' [ɔˈɦɔ] shows two rules of the opening units at once. The 'г' between the vowels is the voiced [ɦ], never [ɡ], and the unstressed first 'о' keeps its full rounded sound, because Ukrainian 'о' is never reduced. 'Ой' [ɔj] is one syllable, so it carries no stress mark.

The other particles:

- In 'невже́' [nɛwˈʒɛ] the 'в' ends the first syllable before the consonant 'ж', so it is the [w] of 'Львів' and 'чита́в'.
- In 'адже́' [ɑˈd͡ʒɛ] the 'дж' is one sound, as in 'jam'.
- In 'хіба́' the 'х' is said a little softer before 'і', as every consonant is.
- 'Таки́' [tɑˈkɪ] and 'таки́й' [tɑˈkɪj] differ only in the final 'й', which must be heard.

The new words of the idioms and proverbs:

- 'Би́ти' has the apostrophe in its present forms, 'б’ю', 'б’єш', 'б’є', 'б’ємо́', 'б’єте́', 'б’ють', as 'пи́ти' does in 'п’ю': the apostrophe keeps the 'б' hard and the [j] of 'ю' and 'є' sounded. The imperative is 'бий', 'би́йте'.
- 'Язи́к' moves its stress to the ending in its other forms: 'язика́'. 'Зуб' does the same in the plural cases other than the nominative: 'зу́би', but 'зуба́ми'.
- 'Тихі́ше' is the adverb 'ти́хо' with the comparative suffix '-іш-' of 'теплі́ший' and the adverb ending '-е' of 'шви́дше', and the stress moves to the suffix. 'Да́лі', further, is the irregular comparative of 'дале́ко'.
- In 'посі́єш' [pɔˈsʲijɛʃ] the 'с' is soft before 'і', and 'є' after the vowel 'і' is [jɛ].
- 'Прислі́в’я' [prɪsˈlʲiʋjɑ] has the apostrophe after 'в' before 'я', so the 'в' stays hard and the 'я' is [jɑ]; the 'л' is soft before 'і'.
- 'Додо́му' is written as one word, because 'до' and 'до́му' have fused into an adverb, and it keeps the stress of 'до́му'.
- 'Гоп' begins with the voiced [ɦ] of 'г', and its final 'п' is [p].
- 'Байдики́' is stressed on its last syllable, and 'розли́ти' on 'ли', like 'ли́ти'.

culture.title: Proverbs, sayings and the people who collected them
culture.text:
Ukrainian distinguishes two kinds of traditional wisdom:

- 'прислі́в’я', a proverb: a complete sentence with a lesson, such as 'Що посі́єш, те й пожне́ш.'
- 'при́казка', a saying: a short fixed phrase without a lesson of its own, often a comparison, such as 'як ри́ба у воді́'

Many of them come from village life: sowing and reaping, the forge, the river and the farm animals. Others mention the seasons, the church calendar and the Cossacks. In the nineteenth century writers and scholars began to collect them, as part of an effort to record the spoken language of ordinary people. Matvii Nomys published a collection of more than fourteen thousand proverbs and sayings in 1864. The writer Ivan Franko gathered tens of thousands more in Galicia, the region around Lviv, and published them in several volumes between 1901 and 1910. These collections are still printed, and Ukrainian schoolchildren study proverbs in their language lessons.

In daily life proverbs are heard most often from older people, who use them to give advice without seeming to lecture: the proverb speaks, not the grandmother. A well-known proverb is often cut short, so 'Тихі́ше ї́деш...' is enough, and the listener supplies the rest. Journalists and advertisers like to change one word of a famous proverb in a headline, which works only because every reader knows the original.

Idioms and particles are a mark of fluent speech, and Ukrainians notice when a foreigner uses them well. They notice just as quickly when one is used in the wrong place: an informal idiom in a job interview sounds as odd in Ukrainian as slang does in an English cover letter. The safest course is to try a new idiom first with friends, who will say whether it fits, and to keep formal speech and writing plain.

paragraphs.target: Ви коли́сь помі́чали, скі́льки твари́н живе́ в на́шій мо́ві? Ко́жен украї́нець зна́є, що означа́є почува́тися як ри́ба у воді́: це коли́ вам ле́гко й до́бре, бо ви на своє́му мі́сці.
paragraphs.source: Have you ever noticed how many animals live in our language? Every Ukrainian knows what it means to feel like a fish in water: it is when you feel easy and good, because you are in the right place.
paragraphs.source_literal: You ever noticed, how-many of-animals lives in our language? Every Ukrainian knows, what means to-feel like fish in water: this when to-you easy and good, because you on own place.

paragraphs.target: Ча́сто в ідіо́мах є части́ни ті́ла. Тому́, хто бага́то гово́рить, ра́дять трима́ти язика́ за зуба́ми. Коли́ на щось нема́є ча́су, ка́жуть: «Ру́ки не дохо́дять».
paragraphs.source: Idioms often contain parts of the body. People who talk a lot are advised to keep their mouths shut. When there is no time for something, people say, 'I can't get around to it.'
paragraphs.source_literal: Often in idioms there-are parts of-body. To-that, who much talks, they-advise to-hold tongue behind teeth. When for something there-is-not of-time, they-say: «Hands not reach».

paragraphs.target: Твари́ни живу́ть і в і́нших ідіо́мах. Коли́ чого́сь ду́же ма́ло, ка́жуть: «Гро́шей у ме́не як кіт напла́кав». А про те, чого́ ніко́ли не бу́де, ка́жуть: «Коли́ рак на горі́ сви́сне».
paragraphs.source: Animals live in other idioms too. When there is very little of something, people say, 'I have next to no money.' And about something that will never happen, people say, 'When the crayfish whistles on the mountain.'
paragraphs.source_literal: Animals live also in other idioms. When of-something very little, they-say: «Of-money at me as cat cried». And about that, of-what never not will-be, they-say: «When crayfish on mountain will-whistle».

paragraphs.target: Як ви́вчити ці ідіо́ми? Слу́хайте, як гово́рять лю́ди в метро́, у кафе́ й на ри́нку, і повто́рюйте те, що чу́єте. Ті́льки не вивча́йте їх усі́ за оди́н ти́ждень: тихі́ше ї́деш, да́лі бу́деш.
paragraphs.source: How do you learn these idioms? Listen to how people talk in the metro, in cafés and at the market, and repeat what you hear. Just don't try to learn them all in one week: more haste, less speed.
paragraphs.source_literal: How to-learn these idioms? Listen, how talk people in metro, in café and on market, and repeat that, what you-hear. Only not learn them all within one week: quieter you-go, further you-will-be.

paragraphs.target: Ну от, слу́хайте. Мій та́то ду́же лю́бить лови́ти ри́бу. Ко́жної субо́ти він ї́здив на о́зеро, і ко́жної субо́ти приїжджа́в додо́му без ри́би.
paragraphs.source: Well, listen. My dad really loves fishing. Every Saturday he went to the lake, and every Saturday he came home without any fish.

paragraphs.target: Ма́ма завжди́ пита́ла: «Ну, де ж на́ша ри́ба?» А він їй: «Сього́дні ри́ба не хоті́ла». Ми смія́лися, а та́то ка́зав, що ми нічо́го не розумі́ємо.

paragraphs.target: І от мину́лої субо́ти він таки́ приві́з ри́бу. Ого́, яку́ вели́ку! Ма́ма не могла́ пові́рити: «Невже́ ти сам її́ спійма́в?» А та́то ті́льки посміха́вся: «Хіба́ ти сумніва́лася?»

Dad bought fish at the market.
Dad went fishing and came home without any fish.
questions.explanation: 'Ко́жної субо́ти він ї́здив на о́зеро, і ко́жної субо́ти приїжджа́в додо́му без ри́би.'

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator use 'таки́' in 'він таки́ приві́з ри́бу'?
choices: Because after so many Saturdays without fish, he finally brought one, against everyone's expectations
Because he brought a fish of that kind
Because he also brought a second fish
questions.explanation: 'Таки́' says that something happened despite doubts. It is not 'таки́й', such, which would agree with 'ри́ба'.

questions.prompt: What did Mom find in Dad's jacket?
questions.explanation: 'Ма́ма знайшла́ в його́ ку́ртці чек із ри́нку.' The fish came from the market, not from the lake, which is why she now reminds him not to forget the receipt.

exercises.prompt: Match the idioms with their meanings
Match the particles and interjections with their meanings

exercises.explanation: Its words say 'to beat baidyky', but the idiom means doing nothing when you should be working.

exercises.prompt: What do the words of 'ки́нути о́ком' literally say?
exercises.explanation: 'Ки́нути' is 'to throw', and 'о́ком' is the instrumental of 'о́ко', eye, the means. The idiom means 'to glance'.

exercises.prompt: At a concert you see a huge, impressive crowd. Which interjection fits?
exercises.explanation: 'Ого́' expresses admiring surprise at something big or numerous. 'Ой' expresses sudden surprise, fright, pain or dismay, and 'ну' is a particle, not a cry of surprise.

exercises.prompt_target: Окса́на в університе́ті почува́ється як ри́ба у ___.
exercises.hint_source: Oksana is in her element at the university.
exercises.explanation: The idiom is 'як ри́ба у воді́', with 'вода́' in the locative after 'у'.

exercises.prompt_target: Вони́ завжди́ ра́зом, їх водо́ю не ___.
exercises.hint_source: They are always together; they are inseparable.
exercises.explanation: The idiom is 'водо́ю не розли́ти', literally 'by-water not to-pour-apart', with the friends as the object 'їх'.
'Да́ти собі́ ра́ду', literally 'to give oneself counsel', means 'to manage'. Without a negation 'ра́да' is in the accusative, 'ра́ду'.
The particle follows 'я', which ends in a vowel, so it is written 'ж'.

exercises.hint_source: He knows about it, after all.
exercises.explanation: The particle follows 'він', which ends in a consonant, so it is written 'же'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'ти ж' but 'він же'?
choices: The particle is written 'ж' after a vowel and 'же' after a consonant.
'Ти' is said to one person and 'він' is about another.
'Же' is used about men and 'ж' about women.
exercises.explanation: It is the same euphony that gives 'б' and 'би': 'ти' ends in a vowel and 'він' in a consonant.

choices: Have you really finished work already?
Have you really started work already?
Have you really finished the book already?

exercises.prompt: 'Хіба́ ти не зна́єш?' What does the speaker expect?
choices: That you do know, and the speaker is surprised that you might not
Nothing: it is a neutral question
exercises.explanation: 'Хіба́' expects the answer opposite to the words: the words say 'you don't know', so the speaker expects that you do.

choices: A particle saying that she came despite doubts or obstacles
exercises.explanation: 'Таки́' is a particle and never changes. The pronoun 'таки́й' ends in 'й' and agrees with a noun.

exercises.prompt_target: Ми ___ всти́гли на по́їзд, хоча́ таксі́ до́вго не було́.
exercises.hint_source: We made the train after all, although the taxi took a long time to come.
exercises.explanation: 'Таки́' stands before the verb and says that it happened despite the obstacle, here the late taxi. 'Все-таки́' is also correct.

exercises.hint_source: The shops are closed; it's Sunday today, after all.
exercises.explanation: 'Адже́' gives a reason that the listener already knows, which is what 'after all' says. 'Бо' is also correct: it gives the cause without that shade of meaning.

exercises.prompt: In a conversation, what does 'Я до Оле́ни.' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'До' with the genitive shows a direction, so the verb of motion is understood and left out. 'At Olena's' is 'у Оле́ни'.

choices: Right, I've arrived, see you tomorrow!
Right, I'm off, see you on Sunday!
Right, I'm off, see you tomorrow!

exercises.prompt: Which sentence puts 'nice' first for emphasis?
exercises.explanation: In speech the word that carries the feeling comes first. The first sentence is neutral, and the third puts 'ку́ртка' first.
'От' sums up, and the particle 'і' underlines 'все': literally 'there also all'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Не кажи́ гоп, по́ки не переско́чиш', what does 'по́ки не' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'По́ки не' with a perfective verb means 'until', and its 'не' negates nothing. Without 'не', 'по́ки' means 'while', as in 'Куй залі́зо, по́ки гаря́че.'

exercises.prompt: In 'Що посі́єш, те й пожне́ш', what is 'й'?
exercises.explanation: The proverb has only one verb in each half, so 'й' joins nothing. It is the particle 'і' after a vowel, underlining the pointing word 'те'.

exercises.prompt: In 'Хто ра́но встає́, тому́ Бог дає́', what is 'тому́'?
choices: The dative of 'той': to that one
exercises.explanation: 'Хто' in the first half is picked up by a form of 'той' in the second, and 'дава́ти' needs the person in the dative: 'тому́', to that one.

choices: It ends a syllable before a consonant, as in 'Львів'.
exercises.explanation: The first syllable of 'невже́' ends after the 'в'. A 'в' at the end of a syllable is [w], as in 'Львів' and 'чита́в'.

exercises.prompt: Sam is writing a letter to an employer. Which sentence suits the letter?
choices: Я ніко́ли не б’ю байдики́ на робо́ті.
exercises.explanation: A formal letter uses plain, full sentences. 'Ну' and 'ж' belong to conversation, and 'би́ти байдики́' is an informal idiom.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why does Taras question Sam's 'я ці́лі вихідні́ бив байдики́'?
choices: Sam was at a concert all weekend.
Sam worked hard all weekend, but the idiom means doing nothing.
exercises.explanation: Sam learned twenty idioms, and Taras points out: 'Би́ти байдики́ означа́є нічо́го не роби́ти.'

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why did nobody tell Oksana about Sofiia's new job?
choices: Sofiia asked her friends to keep quiet about it.
exercises.explanation: Olena says: 'Со́фія проси́ла, щоб ми трима́ли язика́ за зуба́ми.' Then she tells Oksana everything anyway.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, what does Iryna Petrivna advise Sam to do?
choices: Write about his experience, and save the idioms for his friends
Put as many idioms as possible into the letter
Learn a hundred idioms in a week
exercises.explanation: She says 'Пиші́ть про свій до́свід' and suggests five idioms a week, not a hundred: 'Тихі́ше ї́деш, да́лі бу́деш.'

exercises.prompt_source: Keep your mouth shut. (to a friend)
He found the keys after all. (with 'таки́')
exercises.explanation: 'Таки́' stands before the verb it stresses. 'Усе́-таки́' is also possible; after the consonant of 'він' it is spelled with 'у'.

exercises.prompt_source: Did you really win? (to a male friend, with 'невже́')
exercises.explanation: 'Невже́' opens the question and shows surprise at something that seems to be true. The past form 'ви́грав' agrees with a man.

exercises.prompt_source: I'm off home. (spoken, with no verb)
exercises.explanation: In speech the verb of motion is left out, because 'додо́му', home as a direction, already shows that you are going.

exercises.prompt_source: Take a look at this menu. (to a friend, with the idiom)
exercises.explanation: 'Кинь' is the imperative of 'ки́нути' for someone you call 'ти', and what you look at follows 'на' with the accusative; 'меню́' never changes.
